categories.name: Infectious diseases
categories.description: Illnesses caused by organisms such as bacteria, viruses and parasites. They pass between people, through food or water, or through the bites of insects. Many are preventable and treatable when they are found early.

categories.name: Chronic conditions
categories.description: Long-term conditions that persist over months or years and are managed day to day. They are usually helped by healthy habits, regular check-ups and, when needed, long-term medicine.

categories.name: Respiratory conditions
categories.description: Conditions that affect the lungs and airways. They range from long-term conditions such as asthma to short-term infections of the chest, and they affect how well oxygen gets into the blood.

diseases.name: Malaria
diseases.shortSummary: Malaria is a serious but preventable and treatable illness spread by mosquito bites. Early testing and treatment make a big difference.
diseases.description: Malaria is a life-threatening disease caused by Plasmodium parasites, passed to people through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. It is preventable and treatable, and early diagnosis and treatment reduce illness, prevent deaths and help reduce spread.
symptoms: Fever, headache and chills, which can be mild and easy to mistake for other illnesses
Vomiting
Symptoms usually start 10 to 15 days after the bite
Milder symptoms in people who have had malaria before
Extreme tiredness
Impaired consciousness
Repeated convulsions
Difficulty breathing
Dark or bloody urine
Jaundice
Abnormal bleeding
causes: Infection with Plasmodium parasites carried by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito
Blood transfusions that have not been screened
Sharing needles that have been contaminated
riskFactors: Children under 5 years old
Pregnant people
People living with HIV/AIDS or another weakened immune system
Travellers who have never had malaria before
Living in or travelling to areas where malaria is common
Sleeping without mosquito protection
prevention: Insecticide-treated bed nets, insect repellent and protective clothing
Indoor residual spraying in areas where malaria is common
The RTS,S vaccine for children in moderate to high transmission areas
Preventive medicines for certain groups, such as pregnant women, young children and travellers, under health-worker guidance
Clearing standing water around the home where mosquitoes can breed

remedy.overview: Malaria always needs treatment with medicine. For the most common dangerous type, the best available treatment is artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT). The right medicine depends on the type of malaria and the person affected, and must be chosen by a health professional.
careOptions: Get tested as early as possible so the right treatment can be started
Take the medicine a health professional prescribes, following their instructions
Finish the full course of treatment even after you feel better
Rest at home and drink plenty of fluids while you recover
precautions: Do not use leftover medicine or medicine that has not been prescribed for you
Do not assume every fever is malaria; a blood test confirms the diagnosis
Keep using mosquito protection during recovery so you are not bitten again
urgentSigns: Extreme tiredness, confusion, repeated convulsions, difficulty breathing, dark or bloody urine, jaundice or abnormal bleeding need emergency care right away
Seek prompt testing for fever in a child, a pregnant person or someone with a weak immune system
Seek care if fever starts after visiting an area where malaria is common
Seek care if symptoms do not improve after starting treatment
remedy.source: World Health Organization malaria fact sheet and health topic pages; checked against NCDC guidance

diseases.name: Typhoid fever
diseases.shortSummary: Typhoid fever is a bacterial illness spread through contaminated food or water. Safe water, carefully prepared food and regular handwashing prevent most cases.
diseases.description: Typhoid fever is an illness caused by Salmonella Typhi bacteria. People pick it up by eating food or drinking water that has been contaminated with the bacteria, or through close contact with someone who has it. The illness usually starts slowly, with a fever that rises over several days. Most people recover fully with the right care, but complications can become serious when the illness is not treated, so medical care is important.
symptoms: Fever that rises gradually over several days
Headache and tiredness
Stomach pain
Constipation or diarrhoea
Loss of appetite and weight loss
A raised, spotty rash on the chest and abdomen in some people
causes: Eating food or drinking water contaminated with infected faeces
Close contact with a person who has typhoid fever
riskFactors: Living in or travelling to an area where sanitation is limited
Drinking water from an unsafe source
Eating food prepared or stored in unhygienic conditions
Children under five years old
prevention: Drink safe water from a piped, treated or properly boiled source
Wash hands thoroughly with soap before eating and after using the toilet
Eat food that is cooked thoroughly and served hot
Avoid raw shellfish and food sold where hygiene is not clear
Get the typhoid vaccine before travelling to high-risk areas

diseases.name: Hypertension
diseases.shortSummary: Hypertension is high blood pressure. It usually gives no symptoms, so regular checks are the only way to know. Treatment lowers the risk of stroke and heart disease.
diseases.description: Hypertension means the pressure of blood against the walls of the arteries stays higher than it should over time. It usually develops slowly and rarely causes symptoms, so many people have it without knowing. Because it does not announce itself, it is often called a silent condition. Untreated high blood pressure makes the heart work harder and raises the long-term risk of stroke, heart attack, kidney disease and problems with eyesight. Simple lifestyle changes and, when needed, medicine keep it under control.
symptoms: Usually no symptoms at all, which is why it is called a silent condition
Headache, especially in the morning, in some people
Blurred vision or seeing spots of light
Shortness of breath
Dizziness or feeling unsteady
Nosebleeds in some people
causes: The arteries narrow and lose their natural elasticity as we age
Certain medical conditions, such as kidney disease, thyroid disease or diabetes
Some medicines, including certain painkillers and steroid medicines
riskFactors: Being overweight
Eating a lot of salt
Not being physically active
Smoking
Drinking too much alcohol
Having a close family member with high blood pressure
prevention: Cut back on salt and avoid processed foods that are high in it
Stay physically active for at least 30 minutes on most days
Keep a healthy weight
Limit alcohol and stop smoking
Eat a diet rich in fruit, vegetables and whole grains
Have your blood pressure checked regularly, even when you feel well

remedy.overview: High blood pressure is usually managed with lifestyle changes, and with medicine when those changes are not enough. A health professional decides whether medicine is needed and which one to use, based on your readings and your overall health. Treatment aims to bring blood pressure to a safe range and to lower the long-term risk of stroke and heart disease.
careOptions: Have your blood pressure checked regularly and keep a record of the readings
Take prescribed medicine every day, even on days when you feel fine
Reduce salt, eat more fruit and vegetables, and stay active
Keep a healthy weight and limit alcohol
Ask a health professional to review your medicines regularly
precautions: Do not stop taking prescribed medicine because you feel well; high blood pressure rarely gives warnings
Do not take someone else’s blood pressure medicine or double a missed dose without advice
Be careful with over-the-counter painkillers and decongestants, which can raise blood pressure
Do not rely on home readings alone; have them checked properly at least once a year
urgentSigns: A severe headache with sudden changes in vision needs emergency care right away
Chest pain, breathlessness, or weakness on one side of the body needs emergency care
A reading of 180 over 120 or higher should be repeated after a few minutes and reported to a health professional
remedy.source: World Health Organization blood pressure fact sheet; checked against NCDC guidance

diseases.name: Type 2 diabetes
diseases.shortSummary: Type 2 diabetes means the body does not use insulin well, so blood sugar stays too high. It is common, often has no early symptoms, and is managed with food, activity and medicine.
diseases.description: Type 2 diabetes is a long-term condition in which the body does not respond properly to insulin, the hormone that helps sugar move from the blood into the body’s cells. As a result, blood sugar levels stay higher than they should. It usually develops gradually and often has no symptoms in the early years, so it is commonly found during a routine check. Over time, high blood sugar can harm the eyes, kidneys, nerves and feet. It can be improved substantially with healthy food, regular activity, weight management and, when needed, medicine.
symptoms: Needing to pass urine often, especially at night
Feeling very thirsty and drinking a lot
Feeling unusually tired or low on energy
Blurred vision
Slow-healing cuts and sores
Tingling or numbness in the hands and feet
Itchy infections that keep coming back, such as thrush
Fever or shivering alongside a wound infection or a foot ulcer
causes: The body gradually becomes resistant to insulin
The pancreas makes less insulin than the body needs
Both together, which is the usual pattern
riskFactors: Being overweight or carrying extra weight around the waist
Being physically inactive
Having a parent, brother or sister with type 2 diabetes
Having high blood pressure or high cholesterol
Being over 45 years old
Having had diabetes during a previous pregnancy
prevention: Keep a healthy weight, and lose a little weight if you are overweight
Be physically active for at least 30 minutes on most days
Eat more vegetables, whole grains and beans, and less refined sugar and sugary drinks
Limit heavily processed and fried foods
Keep blood pressure and cholesterol under control
Have regular blood sugar checks if a close family member has diabetes

remedy.overview: Type 2 diabetes is managed mainly through food, activity and weight management, with medicine added when those steps are not enough. A health professional confirms the diagnosis and decides which treatment suits each person. Early and steady control lowers the risk of eye, kidney, nerve and foot problems, and most people with type 2 diabetes live full, active lives.
careOptions: Follow a balanced eating plan and keep portion sizes steady through the day
Build up to at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week
Take prescribed medicine as directed and do not change the dose without advice
Check your blood sugar as you have been taught and record the readings
Have regular checks of your eyes, feet, kidneys and blood sugar
precautions: Do not take prescribed medicine less often or skip doses, even when you feel well
Do not eat a carbohydrate-rich food without counting it if you have been taught to count carbohydrates
Check your feet every day and get any sore or blister looked at quickly
Never use over-the-counter herbal products for blood sugar without asking a health professional
urgentSigns: Very high blood sugar with vomiting, deep breathing and a fruity smell on the breath needs emergency care right away
A wound on the foot that is black, spreading red or leaking pus needs same-day medical attention
A severe headache with sudden changes in vision needs emergency care
Sudden numbness or weakness on one side of the body needs emergency care
remedy.source: World Health Organization diabetes fact sheet; checked against NCDC guidance

diseases.name: Asthma
diseases.shortSummary: Asthma is a long-term condition of the airways. Symptoms come and go, and with the right treatment most people can stay active and in control.
diseases.description: Asthma is a condition in which the airways in the lungs become narrow and inflamed, sometimes with extra mucus. The airways are then more sensitive, and they react to things like dust, smoke, cold air, pollen or exercise. Symptoms tend to come and go in episodes, and between episodes the lungs can work normally. Asthma cannot be cured, but with the right medicines, an action plan and avoiding triggers, most people can control it well and stay active.
symptoms: Wheezing, a whistling sound when breathing
A tight chest and shortness of breath
Coughing, worse at night or early in the morning
Using a reliever inhaler more often than usual
causes: The airways in the lungs become inflamed and narrow
The airways become overly sensitive to everyday triggers
Family history and exposure to smoke or pollution make it more likely
riskFactors: Having a parent or sibling with asthma or an allergy condition
Having another allergic condition such as hay fever or eczema
Being exposed to smoke, fumes or damp in the home
Living in a city with heavy air pollution
Being a child or a young adult, when asthma is most common
prevention: Avoid cigarette smoke and other smoke exposure
Know your triggers and reduce exposure to them where you can
Use preventer medicine every day as prescribed, even when you feel well
Follow a written asthma action plan and keep it up to date
Have regular reviews with a health professional and check your inhaler technique

remedy.overview: Asthma is controlled with medicines that reduce swelling in the airways and medicines that relax them quickly during an episode. Most people use two inhalers: a preventer used every day, and a reliever used when symptoms appear. A health professional should confirm the diagnosis and write a personal action plan, because the treatment each person needs depends on how often symptoms occur and how severe they are. With the right plan, most people with asthma stay well and stay active.
careOptions: Use your preventer inhaler every day, even on days you feel completely well
Carry your reliever inhaler with you and use it as your action plan describes
Check your technique with a health professional, because small mistakes reduce how well the medicine works
Follow a written asthma action plan and keep it somewhere easy to find
Have regular reviews so the plan can be adjusted if your symptoms change
precautions: Do not stop using your preventer inhaler when you feel better; it works by preventing symptoms
Do not use someone else’s inhaler, even if it is for the same condition
Do not smoke, and avoid smoke and strong fumes around your airways
Do not rely on a reliever inhaler alone if you need it more often than your plan allows; that means the plan needs review
urgentSigns: Breathlessness that makes speaking or eating difficult needs emergency care right away
A reliever inhaler that is not helping within the time your action plan allows needs emergency care
Blue lips or fingertips, confusion or drowsiness during an attack needs emergency care
A tight chest with pain, or a sudden worsening of breathlessness, needs emergency care
remedy.source: World Health Organization asthma fact sheet; checked against NCDC guidance
